title: AI construction estimating: what it does and how to test it
description: How AI reads plans and builds a cost estimate, the standard accuracy ranges for each estimate stage, and how to test it against jobs you already priced.
summary: AI estimating tools read drawings and specifications, count quantities and apply your costs to draft a price. A good estimator still reviews it. Speed matters most when you bid many jobs and win only a few.

example.input: A set of floor plans and specifications for a small office renovation, plus your current labor and material prices.
example.output: A draft estimate with quantities by trade, the unit prices used, a total, and a list of items the tool could not read from the drawings.

howToTest: Choose 10 finished jobs where you know the final cost, and hide the final cost from the tool.
Run each job's drawings through the tool and compare its total with what the job actually cost.
Compare the tool's quantities line by line with your estimator's takeoff. Wrong quantities are the usual root of wrong totals.
Note which items it missed entirely, such as scope buried in the specifications.
Time the work: hours for the tool plus review versus hours for your estimator from scratch.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when your jobs are common building types and you want faster takeoffs from standard drawings.
buyVsBuild.build: Build when you price special products or processes from your own history and want a model tuned to your own past jobs.

watchOuts: Accuracy depends on how complete the design is. An ASTM-based table used by Alberta Infrastructure gives a typical range of minus 30% to plus 50% for the earliest stage and minus 3% to plus 10% for the most complete stage. AI does not remove that gap.
Your own price data is the main input. Old or wrong unit costs give wrong totals.
Never let a draft estimate go out as a bid without an estimator's review.
Note your assumptions and exclusions in writing on every estimate.
